title: The Cyclists and the Fishing Reels
text:
Norman Triplett, a psychologist at Indiana University and a keen cycling fan, noticed something in the official racing records of the League of American Wheelmen. Riders who raced against the clock alone were slower than riders who had a pacer, and both were slower than riders in head-to-head races. Cyclists had theories about suction behind the pacer or worry while leading, but Triplett suspected that the presence of another rider itself spurred people on.

To test this, he built an apparatus with two fishing reels. Turning a reel drew a silk band around a loop, and a flag on the band showed progress. Triplett had about forty children wind the reel as fast as they could, sometimes alone and sometimes side by side with another child doing the same task.

Many children wound faster when competing with another child. Some did not change, and a few did worse, which Triplett put down to overexcitement. He published his findings in 1898, and the study is often cited as one of the first experiments in social psychology, an early look at how merely working next to others changes how we perform.
lesson: Working alongside others can lift your pace. If a task drags, try doing it next to someone who is working hard too.
source: Triplett, N. (1898). The dynamogenic factors in pacemaking and competition. American Journal of Psychology, 9(4), 507-533.
caveat: A modern statistical reanalysis of Triplett's data found the effect among the children weaker than textbooks often suggest.
